claim: BTB (bric-a-brack, Tramtrack, and broad complex) is a diverse group of protein-protein interaction domains found within metazoan proteins.
source: BTB (bric-a-brack, Tramtrack, and broad complex) is a diverse group of protein-protein interaction domains found within metazoan proteins.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that establishes the nature of BTB domains.

claim: Transcription factors contain a dimerizing BTB subtype with a characteristic N-terminal extension.
source: Transcription factors contain a dimerizing BTB subtype with a characteristic N-terminal extension.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The Tramtrack group (TTK) is a distinct type of BTB domain, which can multimerize.
source: The Tramtrack group (TTK) is a distinct type of BTB domain, which can multimerize.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Single-particle cryo-EM microscopy revealed that the TTK-type BTB domains assemble into a hexameric structure consisting of three canonical BTB dimers connected through a previously uncharacterized interface.
source: Single-particle cryo-EM microscopy revealed that the TTK-type BTB domains assemble into a hexameric structure consisting of three canonical BTB dimers connected through a previously uncharacterized interface.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The TTK-type BTB domains are found only in Arthropods.
source: We demonstrated that the TTK-type BTB domains are found only in Arthropods and have undergone lineage-specific expansion in modern insects.
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: TTK-type BTB domains have undergone lineage-specific expansion in modern insects.
source: We demonstrated that the TTK-type BTB domains are found only in Arthropods and have undergone lineage-specific expansion in modern insects.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis data in the manuscript.

claim: The Drosophila genome encodes 24 transcription factors with TTK-type BTB domains.
source: The Drosophila genome encodes 24 transcription factors with TTK-type BTB domains, whereas only four have non-TTK-type BTB domains.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Drosophila genome encodes only four transcription factors with non-TTK-type BTB domains.
source: The Drosophila genome encodes 24 transcription factors with TTK-type BTB domains, whereas only four have non-TTK-type BTB domains.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed that the TTK-type BTB domains have an unusually broad potential for heteromeric associations.
source: Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed that the TTK-type BTB domains have an unusually broad potential for heteromeric associations presumably through a dimer-dimer interaction interface.
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The heteromeric associations of TTK-type BTB domains occur presumably through a dimer-dimer interaction interface.
source: Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed that the TTK-type BTB domains have an unusually broad potential for heteromeric associations presumably through a dimer-dimer interaction interface.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural and interaction data.

claim: BTB was originally found in the Drosophila proteins bric-a-brac, Tramtrack, and broad complex.
source: BTB, also known as POZ (Pox-virus and zinc-finger), is an evolutionarily conserved domain that was originally found in the Drosophila proteins bric-a-brac, Tramtrack, and broad complex (Zollman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: BTB proteins have been identified in poxviruses and eukaryotes.
source: BTB proteins have been identified in poxviruses and eukaryotes, and have various functions including regulation of transcription, chromatin remodeling, cytoskeletal function, ion transport, and ubiquitination/degradation of proteins (Perez-Torrado et al., 2006; Stogios et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BTB proteins have various functions including regulation of transcription, chromatin remodeling, cytoskeletal function, ion transport, and ubiquitination/degradation of proteins.
source: BTB proteins have been identified in poxviruses and eukaryotes, and have various functions including regulation of transcription, chromatin remodeling, cytoskeletal function, ion transport, and ubiquitination/degradation of proteins (Perez-Torrado et al., 2006; Stogios et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BTB domains are 100–120 aa in size.
source: BTB domains are 100–120 aa in size and the core structure consists of five α-helices and three β-strands (Ahmad et al., 1998; Bonchuk et al., 2023; Li et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The core structure of BTB domains consists of five α-helices and three β-strands.
source: BTB domains are 100–120 aa in size and the core structure consists of five α-helices and three β-strands (Ahmad et al., 1998; Bonchuk et al., 2023; Li et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: BTB domains of transcription factors contain an amino-terminal extension that enables homodimerization.
source: In metazoans, BTB domains of transcription factors (commonly referred to as BTB and Zinc Fingers or ZBTB since they are mostly found in combination with C2H2 zinc fingers) contain an amino-terminal extension that enables homodimerization (Ahmad et al., 1998; Ahmad et al., 2003; Bonchuk et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In humans, 156 genes are predicted to encode BTB domain-containing proteins.
source: In humans, 156 genes are predicted to encode BTB domain-containing proteins, of which 49 are transcription factors possessing between 2 and 14 C2H2 domains (Siggs and Beutler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genomic analysis.

claim: In humans, 49 BTB domain-containing proteins are transcription factors possessing between 2 and 14 C2H2 domains.
source: In humans, 156 genes are predicted to encode BTB domain-containing proteins, of which 49 are transcription factors possessing between 2 and 14 C2H2 domains (Siggs and Beutler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous genomic analysis.

claim: In Drosophila, 56 genes are predicted to encode BTB proteins.
source: In Drosophila, 56 genes are predicted to encode BTB proteins, out of which 28 are transcription factors with the BTB domain of the ZBTB subtype (see below).
evidence: This is a finding from genomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In Drosophila, 28 BTB proteins are transcription factors with the BTB domain of the ZBTB subtype.
source: In Drosophila, 56 genes are predicted to encode BTB proteins, out of which 28 are transcription factors with the BTB domain of the ZBTB subtype (see below).
evidence: This is a finding from genomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Drosophila melanogaster genome contains 28 genes encoding transcription factors with BTB domains.
source: The Drosophila melanogaster genome contains 28 genes encoding transcription factors with BTB domains (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from genomic analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The mod(mdg4) locus encodes at least 30 isoforms.
source: The mod(mdg4) locus encodes at least 30 isoforms, most of which have FLYWCH domains (Bradley and Andrew, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Most mod(mdg4) isoforms have FLYWCH domains.
source: The mod(mdg4) locus encodes at least 30 isoforms, most of which have FLYWCH domains (Bradley and Andrew, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The lola locus produces 20 isoforms.
source: Seventeen of the 20 isoforms produced by the lola locus contain different C-terminal C2H2 zinc-fingers (Horiuchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Seventeen of the 20 lola isoforms contain different C-terminal C2H2 zinc-fingers.
source: Seventeen of the 20 isoforms produced by the lola locus contain different C-terminal C2H2 zinc-fingers (Horiuchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A characteristic feature of the TTK-type BTB domain is the presence of the FxLRWN motif at the N-terminal extension.
source: A characteristic feature of the TTK-type BTB domain is the presence of the FxLRWN motif at this N-terminal extension.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 24 BTB domains from Drosophila transcription factors contain the characteristic 'TTK motif'.
source: Comparison of the amino acid sequence of BTBs from 28 Drosophila BTB-containing transcription factors showed that 24 BTB domains contain the characteristic 'TTK motif' (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Four Drosophila transcription factors (CP190, CG6792, CG15725, and Ken) have BTB domains without a TTK motif.
source: Four transcription factors (CP190, CG6792, CG15725, and Ken) have BTB domains without a TTK motif (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: All TTK-type BTB domains can interact with themselves in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: We found that all BTB domains can interact with themselves.
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: 23 out of 24 TTK-type BTB domains interacted with at least one of the GAF, LOLA, or Mod(mdg4) BTB domains.
source: 23 out of 24 TTK-type BTB domains also interacted with at least one of the GAF, LOLA, or Mod(mdg4) BTB domains.
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: GAF, Mod(mdg4), LOLA, and CG8924 all interacted with at least 10 of the 24 TTK-type BTB domains.
source: GAF, Mod(mdg4), LOLA, and CG8924 all interacted with at least 10 of the 24 TTK-type BTB domains, while Chinmo interacted with 18 TTK-type BTB domains (Figure 2c, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid experiments presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 2c.

claim: Chinmo interacted with 18 TTK-type BTB domains.
source: GAF, Mod(mdg4), LOLA, and CG8924 all interacted with at least 10 of the 24 TTK-type BTB domains, while Chinmo interacted with 18 TTK-type BTB domains (Figure 2c, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid experiments presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 2c.

claim: No heteromeric interaction was found between four non-TTK BTB domains (CP190, Ken, CG15275, and CG6792).
source: We also tested the interaction between four non-TTK BTB domains (CP190, Ken, CG15275, and CG6792 (dPLZF)) and did not find heteromeric interaction between them (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The BTBs of CP190 and CG6792 formed homodimers in vitro.
source: The BTBs of CP190 and CG6792 formed homodimers in vitro, like all other classical BTB domains (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from biochemical experiments presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CP190 interacted with GAF and Ribbon in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: Using Y2H, we detected only a small number of interactions between the non-TTK BTB domains of CP190 and Ken with the TTK-type BTB domains: CP190 interacted with GAF and Ribbon, while Ken interacted with Batman and Mamo (Supplementary file 5 and Figure 2—figure supplements 7–11).
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ken interacted with Batman and Mamo in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: Using Y2H, we detected only a small number of interactions between the non-TTK BTB domains of CP190 and Ken with the TTK-type BTB domains: CP190 interacted with GAF and Ribbon, while Ken interacted with Batman and Mamo (Supplementary file 5 and Figure 2—figure supplements 7–11).
evidence: This is a finding from yeast two-hybrid experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Out of 24 TTK-type Drosophila BTB domains, only ten domains were soluble and stable after TEV-cleavage.
source: Out of 24 BTBs, only ten domains were soluble and stable after TEV-cleavage.
evidence: This is a finding from protein expression and purification experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Eight BTB domains appeared as a single peak on size-exclusion chromatography with apparent Mw 90–150 kDa.
source: Eight BTB domains appeared as a single peak on size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) with apparent Mw 90–150 kDa, Batman BTB eluted as a dimer (Figure 3—figure supplements 3–4), while CG32121 BTB formed multiple peaks.
evidence: This is a finding from size-exclusion chromatography experiments presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplements 3–4.

claim: Batman BTB eluted as a dimer on size-exclusion chromatography.
source: Eight BTB domains appeared as a single peak on size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) with apparent Mw 90–150 kDa, Batman BTB eluted as a dimer (Figure 3—figure supplements 3–4), while CG32121 BTB formed multiple peaks.
evidence: This is a finding from size-exclusion chromatography experiments presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplements 3–4.

claim: CG32121 BTB formed multiple peaks on size-exclusion chromatography.
source: Eight BTB domains appeared as a single peak on size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) with apparent Mw 90–150 kDa, Batman BTB eluted as a dimer (Figure 3—figure supplements 3–4), while CG32121 BTB formed multiple peaks.
evidence: This is a finding from size-exclusion chromatography experiments presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplements 3–4.

claim: Only three BTB domains (CG67651-133, CG321211-147, and LOLA1-120) were soluble at concentrations above 5 mg/mL.
source: Only three BTB domains (CG67651-133, CG321211-147, and LOLA1-120) were soluble at concentrations above 5 mg/mL.
evidence: This is a finding from protein expression and purification experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Iterative masked refinement excluding flexible MBP regions resulted in a final reconstruction of core CG67651-133 multimer at a resolution of 3.3 Å.
source: Iterative masked refinement excluding flexible MBP regions resulted in a final reconstruction of core CG67651-133 multimer at a resolution of 3.3 Å (full data processing flowchart is shown at Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from cryo-EM data processing presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cryo-EM map clearly shows the hexameric assembly consisting of three dimers.
source: The map clearly shows the hexameric assembly consisting of three dimers (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a finding from cryo-EM analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: CG6765 hexamer consists of three canonical BTB dimers with extensive hydrophobic molecular contacts and main-chain hydrogen bonds forming a β-sheet between two parallel β4-strands.
source: CG6765 hexamer consists of three canonical BTB dimers with extensive hydrophobic molecular contacts and main-chain hydrogen bonds (N78, V82, Y84, V86) forming a β-sheet between two parallel β4-strands (corresponding to B3 according to Stogios et al., 2005; Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis of the cryo-EM model presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3b and c.

claim: The N-terminal TTK-motif is located within the first β-strand and is involved only in intra-dimer stabilization forming antiparallel beta-sheet with B4.
source: The N-terminal TTK-motif is located within the first β-strand and is involved only in intra-dimer stabilization forming antiparallel beta-sheet with B4 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from structural analysis of the cryo-EM model presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3b.

claim: The Mw determined by SEC-MALS for LOLA was 86.3 kDa, which was 5.7 times larger than the predicted monomeric Mw.
source: The Mw determined by this method was 86.3 kDa, which was 5.7 times larger than the predicted monomeric Mw, and therefore was closest to a hexameric species.
evidence: This is a finding from SEC-MALS experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: MBP-fused LOLA had a MALS-derived Mw of 315 kDa suggesting a monodisperse ~5.6 mer.
source: Consistent with this, we observed that MBP-fused LOLA also had a single symmetrical peak on the SEC profile, and its MALS-derived Mw of 315 kDa suggested a monodisperse (Mw/Mn = 1.000) ~5.6 mer (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding from SEC-MALS experiments presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 4b.

claim: For both CG6765 and LOLA BTBs, the theoretical scattering for hexameric models agreed best with the experimental SAXS data.
source: For both CG6765 and LOLA BTBs, the theoretical scattering for hexameric models agreed best with the experimental data (χ2 values 1.7 and 3.6, respectively Figure 4c and d), while the fits from alternative oligomeric assemblies predicted by AlphaFold were inadequate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is a finding from SAXS analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 4c and d.

claim: SAXS data support that the prevalent oligomer state in the solution of LOLA and CG6765 BTB domains is the hexamer.
source: Thus, SAXS data support that the prevalent oligomer state in the solution of LOLA and CG6765 BTB domains is the hexamer, in accordance with the CryoEM data.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from SAXS and cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All mutations of conserved hydrophobic residues involved in the inter-subunit β-sheet interface led to a strong decrease in protein solubility and the appearance of aggregates in the SEC profiles.
source: In general, all mutations led to a strong decrease in protein solubility and the appearance of aggregates in the SEC profiles (Figure 4—figure supplements 3–6), and often to an inability for self-interaction in Y2H assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 7) suggesting a general impact on protein folding.
evidence: This is a finding from mutagenesis experiments presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplements 3–7.

claim: TTK-type BTB domains were not found outside of Arthropoda.
source: TTK-type BTB domains were not found outside of Arthropoda.
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The most basal clades in which TTK-type BTB domains emerged were Crustaceans and Arachnoidea.
source: The most basal clades in which they emerged were Crustaceans and Arachnoidea (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 5a.

claim: TTK-type BTB domains underwent a lineage-specific expansion in modern phylogenetic groups of insects, to the most extent in Diptera and Hymenoptera.
source: TTK-type BTB domains underwent a lineage-specific expansion in modern phylogenetic groups of insects, to the most extent in Diptera and Hymenoptera.
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The oldest proteins with TTK-type BTBs are LOLA, bric-a-brac2, and Tramtrack.
source: An ortholog search of the 11 best-studied Drosophila TTK-type BTB proteins revealed that the oldest proteins with TTK-type BTBs are LOLA, bric-a-brac2, and Tramtrack, for which orthologs were found in the most basal clades (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from ortholog search presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 5b.

claim: CP190 and CG6792 are the oldest non-TTK Drosophila BTB proteins.
source: The same search for four non-TTK Drosophila BTB proteins revealed that CP190 and CG6792 (a Drosophila PLZF homolog) are the oldest: a CP190 ortholog was found in Nematodes and CG6792 orthologs are present in almost all other Metazoan taxa (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from ortholog search presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 5c.

claim: A CP190 ortholog was found in Nematodes.
source: The same search for four non-TTK Drosophila BTB proteins revealed that CP190 and CG6792 (a Drosophila PLZF homolog) are the oldest: a CP190 ortholog was found in Nematodes and CG6792 orthologs are present in almost all other Metazoan taxa (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from ortholog search presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 5c.

claim: CG6792 orthologs are present in almost all other Metazoan taxa.
source: The same search for four non-TTK Drosophila BTB proteins revealed that CP190 and CG6792 (a Drosophila PLZF homolog) are the oldest: a CP190 ortholog was found in Nematodes and CG6792 orthologs are present in almost all other Metazoan taxa (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from ortholog search presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 5c.

claim: With the exception of Arachnida, in all examined Arthropoda species, the FLYWCH and HTH domains are found only in combination with the TTK-type BTB domains.
source: With the exception of Arachnida, in all examined Arthropoda species, the FLYWCH and HTH domains are found only in combination with the TTK-type BTB domains (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from domain architecture analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: TTK-type BTBs are usually associated with one or two C2H2 domains.
source: Interestingly, TTK-type BTBs are usually associated with one or two C2H2 domains (only MAMO has five C2H2 domains), while mammalian transcription factors commonly have BTB domains in combination with arrays consisting of an average of five C2H2 domains (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a finding from domain architecture analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 6b.

claim: Mammalian transcription factors commonly have BTB domains in combination with arrays consisting of an average of five C2H2 domains.
source: Interestingly, TTK-type BTBs are usually associated with one or two C2H2 domains (only MAMO has five C2H2 domains), while mammalian transcription factors commonly have BTB domains in combination with arrays consisting of an average of five C2H2 domains (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a finding from domain architecture analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 6b.

claim: The mechanism of multimer assembly in TTK-type BTB domains is completely different from that observed in multimeric BTB domains from the T1/KCTD family.
source: Hence the mechanism of multimer assembly is completely different from that observed in multimeric BTB domains from the T1/KCTD family (Figure 3d Ji et al., 2016; Long et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural comparison presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 3d.

claim: The expansion of the TTK-type BTB domains in insects suggests an important but poorly-understood functional role for their ability to form homo- and hetero-multimers.
source: The expansion of the TTK-type BTB domains in insects suggests an important but poorly-understood functional role for their ability to form homo- and hetero-multimers.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on phylogenetic and structural data.

claim: BTB oligomerization mediates strong co-operative binding of GAF to multiple sites but inhibits binding to a single motif.
source: It was shown that BTB oligomerization mediates strong co-operative binding of GAF to multiple sites but inhibits binding to a single motif (Espinás et al., 1999; Katsani et al., 1999) and promotes chromatin loop formation (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BTB oligomerization promotes chromatin loop formation.
source: It was shown that BTB oligomerization mediates strong co-operative binding of GAF to multiple sites but inhibits binding to a single motif (Espinás et al., 1999; Katsani et al., 1999) and promotes chromatin loop formation (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Batman forms complexes with Pipsqueak and GAF by interacting with their BTBs.
source: Batman forms complexes with Pipsqueak and GAF by interacting with their BTBs (Faucheux et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Batman also interacts with the BAB1 BTB domain, and these proteins cooperate in the control of sex combs on male tarsa.
source: Batman also interacts with the BAB1 BTB domain, and these proteins cooperate in the control of sex combs on male tarsa (Gibert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Batman BTB can be recruited to chromatin only through interaction with other DNA-binding BTB proteins.
source: Since the Batman BTB can be recruited to chromatin only through interaction with other DNA-binding BTB proteins, it does not form homomultimers that would prevent it from interaction with other BTBs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure and function of Batman.

claim: The only TTK-type BTB proteins present in both Crustacea and Arachnoidea taxa are Tramtrack orthologs, suggesting that it is the oldest member of the family.
source: The only such proteins present in both taxa are Tramtrack orthologs, suggesting that it is the oldest member of the family.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Cullin3-interacting KLHL BTBs likely are predecessors of ZBTB.
source: Tracing the origin of ZBTB domains using bioinformatic and protein modeling approaches revealed that Cullin3-interacting KLHL BTBs likely are predecessors of ZBTB, evolving of the ZBTB-type N-terminal extension containing β1 element occurred early in metazoan evolution, however, the actual fusion of ZBTB with zinc-fingers in domain architectures happened over the course of evolution of Bilaterian organisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from bioinformatic and modeling analysis.

claim: Evolving of the ZBTB-type N-terminal extension containing β1 element occurred early in metazoan evolution.
source: Tracing the origin of ZBTB domains using bioinformatic and protein modeling approaches revealed that Cullin3-interacting KLHL BTBs likely are predecessors of ZBTB, evolving of the ZBTB-type N-terminal extension containing β1 element occurred early in metazoan evolution, however, the actual fusion of ZBTB with zinc-fingers in domain architectures happened over the course of evolution of Bilaterian organisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from bioinformatic and modeling analysis.

claim: The actual fusion of ZBTB with zinc-fingers in domain architectures happened over the course of evolution of Bilaterian organisms.
source: Tracing the origin of ZBTB domains using bioinformatic and protein modeling approaches revealed that Cullin3-interacting KLHL BTBs likely are predecessors of ZBTB, evolving of the ZBTB-type N-terminal extension containing β1 element occurred early in metazoan evolution, however, the actual fusion of ZBTB with zinc-fingers in domain architectures happened over the course of evolution of Bilaterian organisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from bioinformatic and modeling analysis.

claim: T1 BTBs are associated with the emergence of multicellularity and the need for cell-cell communication.
source: T1 BTBs are associated with the emergence of multicellularity and the need for cell-cell communication (Srivastava et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In humans and mouse, BTB-C2H2 proteins are encoded by at least 49 genes that are important regulators of development and commonly function as sequence-specific repressors of gene expression.
source: In humans and mouse, BTB-C2H2 proteins are encoded by at least 49 genes that are important regulators of development and commonly function as sequence-specific repressors of gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian BTB-C2H2 proteins.

claim: Mammalian BTB-C2H2 proteins usually have many C2H2 domains that recognize extended and specific DNA motifs.
source: In contrast to Arthropoda TTK-type BTB proteins, mammalian BTB-C2H2 proteins usually have many C2H2 domains that recognize extended and specific DNA motifs.
evidence: This is a comparison based on domain architecture analysis.

claim: Many of the TTK-type BTB transcription factors in Arthropods have multiple isoforms with different DNA-binding or protein interaction domains.
source: Despite the fact that mammals have more highly-specific DNA-binding proteins, many of the TTK-type BTB transcription factors in Arthropods have multiple isoforms with different DNA-binding or protein interaction domains which, along with the ability to heteromultimerize, can result in a large diversity of complexes possessing a broad range of DNA-binding specificities.
evidence: This is a finding from domain architecture analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ability of TTK-type BTB transcription factors to heteromultimerize can result in a large diversity of complexes possessing a broad range of DNA-binding specificities.
source: Despite the fact that mammals have more highly-specific DNA-binding proteins, many of the TTK-type BTB transcription factors in Arthropods have multiple isoforms with different DNA-binding or protein interaction domains which, along with the ability to heteromultimerize, can result in a large diversity of complexes possessing a broad range of DNA-binding specificities.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and interaction data.
